comment: Negative verification vectors for buildclamp attestations. Every entry names the
reason the document must be rejected FOR, because a verifier that rejects
everything passes a naive negative suite.
`expect` is either a VerifyError variant name, `not-fully-enforced` for a document
that verifies and must not be reported as a fully enforced run, or `accept` for the
These are unsigned: the free binary checks everything except the signature and says
so. Cryptographic vectors belong wherever the signature is checked.

`given` names the digests a verifier should be handed for that vector. A statement's policy and report hashes appear once each, so nothing internal contradicts them and the rejection needs the file they should have matched.

vectors.why: The control. A negative suite that only contains rejections cannot tell a correct verifier from one that rejects everything, which is the failure this whole file is arranged around.

CVE-2022-35929: cosign returned success when no attestation of the requested type existed, because the type came from a --type flag rather than from the document. A verifier must read predicateType out of the statement. Fixed cosign is >= 1.10.1.
An older in-toto Statement has a different shape — predicate fields moved — so reading it as v1 would produce a document whose fields came from defaults.

The artefact hash appears twice: in `subject[0].digest`, which is what Kyverno, policy-controller and `cosign verify-attestation` match on, and in the predicate, which is what a person reads. This vector makes them differ. A verifier that checked only one would hand two readers different conclusions about the same signature, so the disagreement is itself the rejection — no --artefact needed.
An in-toto Statement with no subject names no artefact: there is nothing for a policy engine to match on and nothing the document could be about.
Two builds under 'the same policy' that hash differently were not under the same policy.
The statement's whole content is a claim about what a report says. A statement pointing at a different report is a claim about a different run.

Parses and verifies; is_fully_enforced() must be FALSE. Every tier says 'enforced:' and every one of them is true about the capabilities that WERE held — while a build script could read every credential file on the host. This is the laundering case.
Same shape: proc-macro expansion ran unheld, which is the half of the threat a build-script-only tool misses entirely, and every tier still says 'enforced:'.
One advisory capability among enforced ones. The summary carries the WEAKEST tier seen across the whole run, so one unit out of two hundred decides this.

An operator switched a mechanism off. The tiers cannot describe a mechanism that did not run — a switched-off one leaves either nothing or a weaker one still reporting 'enforced:' — so the override vetoes the claim before the tiers are read.
A run that recorded no tiers is not a run that enforced everything. `all()` over an empty collection is true, which is the shape of bug this vector exists for.
A strict decoder is the point: two strings a lenient decoder reads as the same payload are two payloads one signature could be replayed across.
The payloadType is part of what DSSE signs, through the PAE encoding. An envelope declaring one type and carrying another is a document two readers disagree about.

A statement from before enforcement_profile existed cannot be read as one that has it, and must not be defaulted into 'both hardenings on' — which is the direction a serde default would have taken it.
Scope is mandatory. A statement that does not say what it did not hold is one whose silence a reader would take for 'nothing'.
